pos: n. (Johannes Comander, c. 1484–1557, reformer of Chur and of the Three Leagues of Rhaetia)
etymology: Comander, a graecised form of his family name Dorfmann, from kome, a village, and aner, a man; Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Johannes Comander was a native of the Grisons who studied at Basel, served parishes in the mountains, and in 1523 was called to St Martin's at Chur, the chief church of the Three Leagues of Rhaetia. From that pulpit he preached the Reformation into a confederation of self-governing Alpine communes in which no prince could impose anything, so that every parish had to be persuaded separately. He drew up the eighteen theses which were disputed at Ilanz in January 1526 before the deputies of the Leagues, and he carried the day; the articles which followed left each commune free to choose its own religion and its own pastor and set Scripture as the test of preaching. For the next thirty years Comander organised what that decision produced: a synod of the Rhaetian churches, an examination of candidates, a church order, correspondence with Zurich and with Bullinger, and the long defence of the Reformed doctrine against both the Roman party and the Italian radicals who came over the passes. He died at Chur in 1557. The dictionary enters him because his Reformation was carried by argument in a free confederation rather than by a prince's decree, which makes Rhaetia the nearest thing in the sixteenth century to the conditions the dictionary itself holds to be proper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a disputation as a contest in argument; a league as a confederacy of states; and a commune as a small territorial division governing itself.

COMMUNE, v.i. [Fr. communier.] To converse together familiarly; as a noun in foreign use, a small territorial district governing its own affairs.
THESIS, n. [Gr. a position.] A position or proposition which a person advances and offers to maintain by argument.
PERSUADE, v.t. [L. persuadeo.] To influence by argument, advice or entreaty; to bring to an opinion by reasoning.

corruption_summary: Reformer of Chur who carried the Rhaetian Reformation by disputation at Ilanz in 1526, in a confederation where no prince could impose it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption, so general in accounts of the German Reformation that it is rarely stated, that a reformation is something a government does. Rhaetia is the counter-example. There was no prince; the Leagues could not decide religion for a commune, and a commune could not decide it for its neighbour; and so the question was settled in each valley by preaching and argument, parish by parish, over a generation. It was slower, it left a permanently mixed country, and it produced convictions rather than conformity.

The principle to recover is the method. “they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) describes a congregation examining a preacher, which is exactly what the Ilanz articles required of the Rhaetian communes. The dictionary holds that this is the proper way a church changes its mind, that it cannot be hurried, and that the uniformity obtained by a decree is not worth what it appears to be worth.

pos: n. (town of the Grisons on the upper Rhine; where the disputations of 1524 and 1526 settled the Rhaetian Reformation)
etymology: German Ilanz, Romansh Glion, from a pre-Roman root; the town is the oldest on the upper Rhine above the gorge.
biblical_def: Ilanz is a small town on the upper Rhine in the Grisons, and twice in three years the deputies of the Three Leagues of Rhaetia met there to settle what their country should believe. At the first disputation, in 1524, the bishop of Chur's party and the reformers argued before the Leagues and nothing was concluded. At the second, in January 1526, Comander's eighteen theses were debated for several days and the reformers were judged to have proved their case from Scripture, the Roman party having largely declined to argue on that ground. The articles the Leagues then enacted are the remarkable part. They did not establish the Reformation. They provided that preaching should be out of the Scriptures and judged by them, that each commune might call and dismiss its own pastor, that the bishop's jurisdiction and courts were restricted, and that monks and nuns might leave their houses and clergy might marry. In other words a political authority settled procedure and left doctrine to the parishes. The dictionary enters Ilanz for that distinction, which almost no other state in Europe managed to draw, and which is close to what the dictionary holds the civil magistrate's proper part to be.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an article as a single clause in a system of regulations; jurisdiction as legal power or authority; and procedure as the manner of proceeding.
webster_full: ARTICLE, n. A single clause in a contract, account, system of regulations or treaty; a particular; a point of faith.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the extent of power or authority.
PROCEDURE, n. [Fr. procedure.] The act or manner of proceeding or moving forward; process; conduct; management.
DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words or by arguments; a public exercise in argumentation.
ENACT, v.t. To make, as a law; to pass, as a bill into a law; to establish by legal and authoritative act.

corruption_summary: Grisons town where the articles of 1526 made Scripture the test of preaching and gave each commune the right to call its own pastor.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption these articles broke was the bishop's ordinary jurisdiction over the parishes of a country—the system by which a pastor was presented to a congregation that had no voice, judged by a court the congregation could not reach, and maintained whether it would hear him or not. The Ilanz articles put the call and the dismissal in the commune's hands and the test of his preaching in the Scriptures, which is substantially the congregational principle.

The principle to recover is the division of the spheres which Ilanz, almost accidentally, respected. The civil power is “the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4) in its own sphere; here it protected a right and declined to dictate a confession. The dictionary holds that this is the magistrate's part—keeping the peace in which the church may argue—and that the German territorial churches, which did the opposite, bought their uniformity at the price of making the gospel a dynastic policy.

pos: n. (Philipp Gallicius, c. 1504–1566, Romansh reformer of the Engadine and author of the Rhaetian Confession)
etymology: Gallicius, a Latinised form of his Romansh name Saluz; Philipp, from Greek Philippos, a lover of horses.
biblical_def: Philipp Gallicius was born in the Munstertal, the Romansh-speaking valley of the eastern Grisons, and he was the reformer of his own people. He preached in the Engadine from the 1520s, in Romansh and in German, through the slow commune-by-commune process the Ilanz articles had made the rule, and he was afterwards called to Chur as Comander's colleague and successor. His chief written work is the Confessio Raetica of 1552, the confession of faith of the Rhaetian churches, a short and plain document which served the Three Leagues as their doctrinal standard; he also wrote a Romansh catechism and liturgy, and he supported the labour of putting the Scriptures into Romansh. He stood with Comander against the Italian radicals—antitrinitarians and anabaptists—who used the Grisons as a corridor and sometimes as a refuge, and he insisted that a country which allowed every commune to choose must still have a confession by which to judge what was being taught. He died at Chur in 1566. The dictionary enters him because a confession written for a people of four languages in thirty self-governing valleys is a harder and more useful work than one written for a court.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith; a liturgy as a form of prayers for public worship; and a dialect as the form of a language peculiar to a province.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; the acknowledgment of a belief.
LITURGY, n. [Gr. public service.] All the prescribed services of a church, as distinct from private devotion; a formulary of public prayers.
DIALECT, n. [Gr. to converse.] The form or idiom of a language peculiar to a province or to a people.
STANDARD, n. That which is established as a rule or measure; a test by which other things are tried.
VERNACULAR, adj. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.

corruption_summary: Romansh reformer of the Engadine, author of the Rhaetian Confession of 1552, who held that a free confederation still needs a standard of doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Gallicius had to meet was antitrinitarianism carried north over the Italian passes, and the dictionary names it as he did. Men who had fled the Inquisition arrived in the Grisons with the doctrine of the Trinity in question, and the commune system which protected the Reformation also protected them; a valley that could call its own pastor could call one who denied the deity of the Son. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) is the first line of the answer, and the Rhaetian Confession exists because freedom without a standard is only a corridor.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that liberty of the congregation and a confession of faith are not alternatives. The dictionary holds congregational government and a subordinate standard together, as the 1689 Confession itself does: the church governs itself and confesses the faith, and the confession is what makes the self-government something other than a drift. “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) presupposes a faith delivered in words that can be written down.

pos: n. (Jachiam Bifrun, 1506–1572, notary of Samedan who printed the first Romansh New Testament in 1560)
etymology: Bifrun, a surname of the Upper Engadine; Jachiam, the Romansh form of Jacob, from Hebrew Ya'aqob, a supplanter.
biblical_def: Jachiam Bifrun was not a minister. He was a notary of Samedan in the Upper Engadine, trained in law at Paris, who held the ordinary offices of a Grisons commune and who undertook, as a layman, to put the New Testament into the Romansh of his own valley. He worked from the Latin and from German and Italian versions, coined the vocabulary he needed in a tongue which had never been used for connected prose of this kind, paid for the printing himself, and brought out at Poschiavo in 1560 the book called in Ladin the New Holy Testament. It is the first printed book in Romansh and the foundation of Romansh as a written language. He also printed a catechism. He received little thanks at the time; the work was criticised for its Latinisms and its borrowings, which is the usual reception of a first translation into any tongue. The dictionary enters Bifrun because of what he was. The doctrine that every man must read the Scriptures for himself was carried out here not by a synod or a prince or a university but by a country lawyer who looked at his neighbours, saw that they could not read the Bible, and spent his own money so that they could.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a notary as an officer who attests deeds and writings; to translate as to render into another language; and a layman as one not in orders, distinguished from the clergy.
webster_full: NOTARY, n. [L. notarius.] An officer authorized to attest and certify deeds and other writings, to make them authentic in another country.
TRANSLATE, v.t. [L. translatus.] To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
LAYMAN, n. [from laity.] A man not in orders; one of the people, as distinguished from the clergy.
VERSION, n. [L. versio.] A translation; that which is rendered from another language; as the common version of the Scriptures.
COIN, v.t. To make or fabricate, as money; hence, to invent or fabricate, as a new word.

corruption_summary: Engadine notary who translated and printed at his own cost the first Romansh New Testament, in 1560, the first printed book in that language.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is clericalism of the quiet sort: the assumption that the work of getting the Scriptures to a people belongs to ministers and committees, and that a layman's part is to pay a subscription. Bifrun is the refutation and he is not unique—the history of Bible translation is full of merchants, notaries, printers and schoolmasters who did the work because nobody else was going to. The dictionary holds the distinction between the office of the ministry and the gifts of the congregation, and denies that the second is idle while the first is at work.

The principle to recover is in Nehemiah's picture of a reading and an explaining: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). A translation is the first half of that, and it has to exist before the second half can be attempted. Bifrun's version was criticised for its borrowings, and every first translation is; a defective version in a man's own tongue is of more use to him than a perfect one in a tongue he does not have.

pos: n. (Ulrich Campell, c. 1510–c. 1582, Engadine pastor, Romansh psalmist and first historian of Rhaetia)
etymology: Campell, Romansh, from Latin campus, a field, with a diminutive; Ulrich, from Germanic uodal, inheritance, and richi, rule.
biblical_def: Ulrich Campell was pastor at Susch and then at Sent in the Lower Engadine for some forty years, and he did three kinds of work which belong together. He served a Romansh-speaking mountain parish, with the preaching, catechising and burying that implies. He put the Psalms into Romansh verse so that his people could sing them, publishing a psalter in 1562 which is among the earliest books in the language and which gave the Engadine churches their singing. And in his old age he wrote, in Latin, the first history and topographical description of Rhaetia, working from documents, inscriptions and his own travel through the valleys, so that the Three Leagues had a record of themselves made before the Thirty Years War destroyed much of the evidence. He died about 1582. The dictionary enters him for the combination, which is the right order of a pastor's labours and is not often found in one man. He gave his congregation the Psalms to sing before he gave his country a history to read, and he wrote the history in the knowledge that his own parish would never read a word of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms; topography as the description of a particular place; and antiquary as one versed in antiquity.
webster_full: PSALTER, n. [L. psalterium.] The book of Psalms; sometimes applied to a version of the Psalms in metre for singing.
TOPOGRAPHY, n. [Gr. place, and to describe.] The description of a particular place, city, town, manor or tract of land.
ANTIQUARY, n. [L. antiquarius.] One who is versed in antiquity; one who studies and collects the relics of ancient times.
METRE, n. [Gr. measure.] Rhythmical arrangement of syllables into verses; the measure of a verse.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a minister; the inhabitants of such a district.

corruption_summary: Lower Engadine pastor for forty years, who gave his people the Psalms in Romansh verse and his country its first written history.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live question is the use of a pastor's time, and the dictionary states the order Campell kept. The psalter came first, because it was for the congregation he was answerable for; the history came in old age, and it was a gift to a country rather than a duty to a parish. A minister who reverses that order—who writes for the public while his own people are untaught—has mistaken a liberty for a calling.

The principle to recover is the place of psalmody in the church's own tongue. “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16) is an instrument of teaching, not an ornament of the service, and it works only in words the people own. “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land” (Psa 137:4) is the exile's complaint; a congregation singing in a tongue it does not speak is in a mild form of the same condition, and Campell saw it and spent years on the remedy.

pos: n. (village of the Upper Engadine in the Grisons; a commune which chose the Reformation by its own vote)
etymology: Romansh Zuoz, from Latin subtus or a related form meaning below or beneath; the village stands on a terrace above the Inn.
biblical_def: Zuoz is a village of the Upper Engadine, high on the Inn above Samedan, and it was the seat of the Planta family, the leading house of the valley. Its interest for the dictionary lies in how it became Reformed. Under the Ilanz articles of 1526 the religion of a Rhaetian commune was decided by the commune: the men of the place assembled, heard the question, and voted, and whichever way the vote went the minority had to live with it. The Engadine villages went over in the 1520s and 1530s one by one in this manner, Zuoz among them, with the altars taken out and the Mass discontinued by resolution of the assembly. It is an uncomfortable procedure to describe. A congregation's doctrine was settled by a show of hands among the heads of households, who were not necessarily converted men, and the result was binding. The dictionary enters Zuoz because the procedure states, in its crudest form, a problem the congregational principle has to answer: a church governed by its members is governed by whoever its members are, and the remedy is not to take the government away but to be careful whom the church receives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vote as an expression of will or preference; an assembly as a company collected together; and a majority as the greater number.
webster_full: VOTE, n. [L. votum.] Suffrage; the expression of a wish, desire, will or preference, in regard to the decision of a question.

corruption_summary: Upper Engadine commune which voted itself Reformed under the Ilanz articles, with the altars removed by resolution of the village assembly.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the confusion of the parish with the church. In the Rhaetian system the commune and the congregation were the same body: every household of the village belonged, and the religion was decided by the village assembly. That gave the valleys the Reformation, and it also meant that a church's doctrine rested on the votes of men who had never professed faith. The same confusion produced, in other countries, the national churches in which baptism and citizenship are one thing; the dictionary names it as an error however convenient its results.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gathered church. “Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls” (Act 2:41) is the order—word received, then baptism, then addition to the body—and the body so gathered is what Scripture calls “the house of God, which is the church of the living God” (1Ti 3:15). A congregation of all the inhabitants is a parish; it becomes a church when its members are believers.

pos: n. (Italian-speaking valley of the Grisons south of the Bernina; seat of the press that printed for the Italian evangelicals)
etymology: Italian Poschiavo, German Puschlav, from Late Latin post clavem or a related form, the place beyond the pass or the key; the valley runs south from the Bernina to the Italian plain.
biblical_def: Poschiavo is the valley which carries the road from the Bernina down into Italy, Italian in speech and Grisons in government, and that double character made it important out of all proportion to its size. Under the Rhaetian settlement its commune was free to choose its religion; a Reformed congregation was established, which has continued to this day, while part of the valley remained Catholic. Because it lay on the Italian side of the Alps and under Swiss law, it became a door. Italian evangelicals came up through it fleeing the Inquisition; Giulio della Rovere served as its pastor; and Dolfino Landolfi set up a press at Poschiavo which printed Italian Protestant books—translations, catechisms, controversial works and, in 1560, Bifrun's Romansh New Testament—for carriage back over the frontier into a country where owning them was a capital matter. The dictionary enters Poschiavo for that trade. The Reformation reached Italy mainly as contraband, in packs on the backs of men going down a valley road, and the places where the books were printed were chosen not for their learning but for their geography.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contraband as prohibited goods; a press as a printing machine; and a frontier as the border of a country.
webster_full: CONTRABAND, adj. [It. contrabbando.] Prohibited; unlawful; as contraband goods, which are either exported from or imported into a country against its laws.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which paper is impressed by types; the art or business of printing.
FRONTIER, n. [Fr. frontiere.] The marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
SMUGGLE, v.t. To import or export secretly goods which are forbidden by the government, or without paying the duties.
PASS, n. A narrow passage, entrance or avenue; a narrow or difficult place of entrance and exit, as a mountain defile.

corruption_summary: Grisons valley on the Italian road whose press printed the Protestant books carried as contraband into Italy, and the Romansh New Testament of 1560.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is a state which makes the possession of a book a capital offence. The Italian Indexes and the Inquisition's tribunals treated the vernacular Scriptures and the Reformers' writings as a contagion to be stopped at the frontier, and men were put to death for carrying them. The dictionary names that policy for what it is: an admission, by the party that held every advantage of power and learning, that it could not answer the books.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Habakkuk gives the prophet: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). The running and the reading belong together. A church which prints and does not distribute has done half the work, and the men who carried packs over the Bernina were doing the other half at the price the law of Italy set on it.

pos: n. (Italian-speaking valley of the Grisons below the Maloja, Italian Val Bregaglia; Reformed from the sixteenth century)
etymology: German Bergell, Italian Bregaglia, from Latin Praegallia, the land before Gaul; the valley runs west from the Maloja pass toward Chiavenna.
biblical_def: The Bergell is the valley which falls from the Maloja pass westward toward Chiavenna, Italian in speech and belonging to the Grisons, with Vicosoprano, Stampa, Soglio and Bondo among its villages. Like Poschiavo it was an Italian-speaking commune under Rhaetian law, and like Poschiavo it went Reformed under the Ilanz settlement and has remained so. Its churches were served in the sixteenth century partly by Italian evangelicals who had come north, so that a congregation of Alpine farmers was preached to in their own tongue by men who had fled the Inquisition at Naples, Venice or Milan. The valley was the route by which much of the Italian evangelical movement reached the Reformed world, and by which some of its less welcome freight also came: the antitrinitarian teachers whom Comander and Gallicius had to answer travelled the same road. The Bergell was also a thoroughfare for armies in the Valtellina wars. The dictionary enters it because it is the clearest instance of the Reformed church's ordinary difficulty with a refugee movement, which is that the same door admits the persecuted brother and the heretic, and no door can be made to admit only one of them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a thoroughfare as a passage through; an asylum as a place of refuge; and discrimination as the act of distinguishing, the power of making distinctions.
webster_full: THOROUGHFARE, n. A passage through; a passage from one street or opening to another; an unobstructed way.
ASYLUM, n. [L. asylum.] A sanctuary or place of refuge, where criminals and debtors shelter themselves; any place of retreat and security.
DISCRIMINATION, n. [L. discriminatio.] The act of distinguishing; the act of making or observing a difference; the faculty of nicely distinguishing.
FREIGHT, n. The cargo or any part of the cargo of a ship; lading; that which is carried.
ADMIT, v.t. [L. admitto.] To suffer to enter; to grant entrance; to receive, as a person or a doctrine.

corruption_summary: Italian-speaking Grisons valley, Reformed and served by Italian exiles, which was also the road by which antitrinitarian teachers came north.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption which came up this valley with the refugees was antitrinitarianism, and the dictionary has named it elsewhere and names it here: the denial of the eternal deity of the Son is not a Christian opinion. What the Bergell adds is the practical difficulty. The men who arrived were in real danger, many were sound, and the valley could not interrogate every traveller; the honest course, which Comander and Gallicius took, was to keep the hospitality and to insist on a confession for anyone who would teach.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing of two duties which are often set against each other. “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) is the church's duty to the persecuted, and it is not qualified by convenience. “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1) is its duty concerning doctrine, and it is not suspended by sympathy. A man may be sheltered as a sufferer and refused as a teacher in the same week, and a church that cannot do both will fail at one of them.

pos: n. (chief town of the Valtellina; seat of a Reformed congregation under Grisons rule until 1620)
etymology: Italian Sondrio, from a Lombard sundrium, a lord's demesne land; the town stands on the Mallero where it enters the Adda.
biblical_def: Sondrio is the chief town of the Valtellina, the long Alpine valley of the upper Adda which the Three Leagues of Rhaetia had taken in 1512 and governed as a subject territory for more than a century. The population was Italian and Catholic; the rulers were Swiss and in the main Reformed; and the Leagues used their authority to establish Reformed congregations in the valley towns, Sondrio among them, with ministers sent down from the Grisons and Italian exiles among the preachers. It was an uneasy arrangement from the first: a minority church planted by a foreign government in a Catholic valley, with the governorships of the valley sold at Chur and the resentment of the subject population accumulating for a hundred years. On the nineteenth of July 1620 that resentment broke out, with Spanish and Austrian encouragement, in a general rising; the Reformed of the valley, ministers and laity together, were hunted and killed over several days in the massacre the Italians call the holy slaughter, and the Reformed church of the Valtellina was extinguished in a week. The dictionary enters Sondrio as the hardest lesson in this batch: a true church was planted in that valley by a method which guaranteed what happened to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a subject territory as a country held in dependence; a governor as one invested with supreme authority in a province; and resentment as the excitement of anger at an injury.
webster_full: SUBJECT, adj. Placed or situated under; being under the power and dominion of another; as a subject province.
GOVERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority to administer or enforce the laws, as of a province.
RESENTMENT, n. [Fr. ressentiment.] The excitement of passion which proceeds from a sense of wrong offered to ourselves or to others.
MINORITY, n. The smaller number; the state of being less than half of the whole.
RISING, n. The act of getting up; an insurrection; a sedition; a tumultuous assembly.

corruption_summary: Chief town of the Valtellina, where a Reformed congregation planted under Grisons rule was destroyed with the whole valley church in July 1620.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is double and the dictionary names both parts. The massacre itself was murder, incited and encouraged by Catholic powers, and no grievance excused it; the men killed at Sondrio and Teglio and in the lower valley died for their religion and belong in the register. And the planting of those congregations was itself a fault: the Leagues used a government over a conquered people to establish a church among them, sold the offices that administered it, and left the gospel in the valley permanently identified with a foreign master and a tax-collector.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the manner of a church's planting is part of its doctrine. A congregation gathered by preaching among a people, in their own tongue, by men who have no power over them, is a church; the same doctrine imposed through a governor is a party. “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) is not a comfortable word here, and the dictionary does not soften it: the Reformed of the Valtellina suffered a crime, and the Leagues had put them where the crime could reach them.

pos: n. (town of the lower Valtellina; seat of a Reformed congregation destroyed in the massacre of 1620)
etymology: Italian Morbegno, of uncertain origin, perhaps from a Lombard personal name; the town stands in the lower Valtellina near the head of Lake Como.
biblical_def: Morbegno is the chief town of the lower Valtellina, at the end of the valley nearest Lake Como and the Milanese frontier, and under the Grisons administration it held one of the Reformed congregations of the valley. Its position made it the most exposed of them: it was the first place reached from Spanish Milan, its Catholic population was in constant contact with the archbishop's clergy across the border, and the Capuchin and Jesuit mission to the valley worked chiefly from this end of it. When the rising came in July 1620 the lower valley moved first, and the congregation at Morbegno was among those destroyed; the ministers who did not escape over the passes were killed with their people. After 1620 the valley was closed to Reformed worship, and the treaties which ended the Valtellina wars confirmed it; no Reformed congregation was restored there. The dictionary enters Morbegno as the companion of Sondrio and for one further point. A frontier congregation is not simply a congregation in a dangerous place. It is the place where a church finds out what it has actually taught, because a people under that kind of pressure either know why they believe what they believe or they do not, and nobody can tell them in the week it is tested.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a body of persons sent to propagate religion; exposed as laid open, unprotected; and extirpation as the act of rooting out.
webster_full: MISSION, n. [L. missio.] A sending or being sent; persons sent; a station of missionaries; the act of sending to propagate religion.
EXPOSED, adj. Laid open; made bare; put in danger; unprotected; not covered or defended.
EXTIRPATION, n. [L. extirpatio.] The act of rooting out; eradication; excision; total destruction.
FRONTIER, n. The border or confine of a country, bordering on another country; the marches.
TREATY, n. [Fr. traite.] An agreement, league or contract between two or more nations or sovereigns, formally signed.

corruption_summary: Lower Valtellina town, the most exposed of the valley's Reformed congregations, destroyed in July 1620 and never restored.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary records what the Valtellina mission actually was on the Catholic side, without either exaggeration or excuse: a sustained, intelligent and well-funded effort by the Capuchins and the Jesuits, working from Milan across a political frontier, to recover a valley by preaching, schools and charity. It largely succeeded before the massacre, and the massacre completed by violence what the mission had begun by argument. Naming the first half honestly is part of naming the second half justly.

The principle to recover is that catechising is the defence of a frontier congregation. “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) is written of a minister, and what is required of the minister has to be worked into the people. “Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you” (1Pe 4:12) is the apostle's warning that the trial is normal; the church which has told its people so, and taught them why, has done what can be done.
